title: The Night Black Like Me's Factory Burned, and the Fortnight After
dek: In November 1993 Herman Mashaba's hair-care factory burned the night before a 24-hour shift, and within two weeks he had bought new premises.

story.event: Rebuilding the hair-care business after its factory near Pretoria was destroyed by fire
story.summary: In November 1993 a fire, suspected to be arson and never solved, destroyed the factory of Black Like Me, the hair-care company Herman Mashaba had co-founded in 1985 with a R30,000 loan. Within two weeks he bought premises in Midrand and rebuilt with savings and a slow, partial insurance payout; he later said the strain led him to sell 75 per cent of the company to Colgate-Palmolive in 1997, and he bought it back in 1999.
paragraphs: On 17 November 1993, by his own account, Herman Mashaba was the last person to leave the Black Like Me factory near Pretoria. He had just spoken to the staff about a 24-hour shift due to start at six the next morning, because, he said later, "we just could not really cope with the demand." At about one or two in the morning he was woken with the news that the factory was on fire. When the workers came for the shift, there was no factory. He remembered people crying.

The company was eight years old. Mashaba, a former travelling salesman, had started it in 1985 with his wife, Connie, Joe Moloantwa and a chemist, Johann Kriel, using R30,000 lent by the businessman Walter Dube and a second backer. Apartheid barred them from operating in so-called white South Africa, so in January 1985 they took a small unit in Ga-Rankuwa, in a homeland, with Kriel dealing with officials. One trade report says the loan, due over three years, was repaid in seven months. By 1990 the firm had built its own plant in nearby Mabopane.

Arson was suspected, and years later the crime was still unsolved. Mashaba's insurers would eventually pay, he said, but slowly, and "I got less than half of the value of what I lost." He knew he had to move fast: "I had no time on my side," he recalled. Within two weeks, drawing on savings and what he could get from the insurers, he bought property in Midrand. He could buy there, he noted, because apartheid's restrictions were collapsing.

The rebuilt business survived, but he later said the fire left it destabilised and in need of a partner. In 1997 he sold 75 per cent to Colgate-Palmolive, keeping a quarter; about two years later, in 1999, he bought it back. Of the fire he said, "I learned a very important lesson of never taking things for granted."

quote.text: brace Thine arm for conflict, nerve thy heart to meet—As things alike to thee—pleasure or pain, Profit or ruin, victory or defeat: So minded, gird thee to the fight
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: Krishna tells a reluctant Arjuna to act, but to hold profit and ruin as alike while he does. Mashaba acted within days, and he has said he keeps his mind fixed on success. The Gita asks for the same speed with less riding on the result, which is harder than it sounds.

reflection: Most losses do not arrive as a fire in the night. They come as a contract that falls through, a colleague who leaves, an illness in the family, a week of work that has to be redone. Mashaba's first move was not a speech about resilience. He found the next building.

When something you depend on goes, it helps to separate two questions: what has to happen in the next fortnight, and what this means for the rest of your life. The first usually has an answer. The second can wait until you have slept, and does not have to be settled on the worst night.
invitation: If something has gone wrong for you recently, write down the single next practical step it needs, and only that. Leave the larger question of what it means for another day.

cross_checks.claim: Black Like Me was founded in 1985 with a R30,000 loan from the businessman Walter Dube
The company's factory was destroyed by fire in November 1993, with arson suspected
Mashaba rebuilt quickly on new premises in Midrand
Colgate-Palmolive held a majority stake from 1997 until Mashaba bought the company back in 1999

research_notes: The slate dated this episode 1985, which is the founding year; the fire was on 17 November 1993 (Mashaba's own date; Bizcommunity and 21 Icons say November 1993), so approx_date is 1993-11. Insurance: Mashaba said in 2015 that the insurers did pay, slowly, and that he received less than half of the value lost; Bizcommunity (2002) says he used a nest egg and 'what he could' from his insurers; 21 Icons says insurance did not compensate for the damage. The story follows Mashaba's account and mentions savings. Location: Bizcommunity and 21 Icons place the burned factory in Mabopane; a 2004 News24 report (blocked to the verifier, so not cited) calls it the Garankuwa plant; the two townships adjoin each other north-west of Pretoria, and the story says 'near Pretoria' for the night and Mabopane for the plant built by 1990. Start-up site: Mashaba's interview says Ga-Rankuwa Industrial Area at one point and Mabopane at another; Bizcommunity and TimesLIVE say Ga-Rankuwa, which the story uses. Colgate: Mashaba links the 1997 sale of 75 per cent to the fire's after-effects, while the 2004 News24 report attributes the partnership to competition from imported brands; the story gives his account as his. The buy-back is dated August 1999 by Mashaba and mid-1999 by Bizcommunity. The second lender is named only as 'uncle Ned' by Mashaba, so the story says 'a second backer'. The repayment in seven months rests on one trade report and is attributed. In 1993 Ga-Rankuwa and Mabopane lay in the Bophuthatswana homeland, inside South Africa's borders; the country is given as South Africa. The Gita lines are Krishna's counsel to Arjuna before battle; the excerpt begins mid-sentence after 'Therefore, arise, thou Son of Kunti!'.
